content: Rotaviruses are a leading cause of viral gastroenteritis and are responsible for more deaths from diarrhoea in children under the age of five than any other single pathogen, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of rotavirus vaccines in preventing rotavirus-induced diarrhoea, associated mortality, and adverse events. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group's trial register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and Biological Abstracts, covering studies up to October 2003. Additional sources included reference lists of relevant articles, as well as direct communication with researchers and vaccine manufacturers. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials comparing rotavirus vaccines to placebo, no intervention, or other rotavirus vaccines in both children and adults. Data extraction and quality assessment were performed independently by two reviewers, who also contacted trial authors for supplementary information. A total of 64 trials involving 21,070 children provided data on the efficacy and safety of three main types of rotavirus vaccines: bovine, human, and rhesus-derived vaccines. The efficacy of these vaccines varied significantly. Depending on the vaccine type, the prevention of a single episode of rotavirus diarrhoea ranged from 22% to 89%. For all-cause diarrhoea, the efficacy ranged from 11% to 44%, while for severe rotavirus diarrhoea, it ranged from 43% to 90%. The rhesus-derived vaccine demonstrated similar efficacy in preventing one episode of rotavirus diarrhoea (37% to 44%) and one episode of all-cause diarrhoea (approximately 15%) in trials conducted in highand middle-income countries. However, data on vaccine-related mortality and safety were limited and incomplete. Significant heterogeneity was observed among the pooled studies, raising concerns about potential bias in the estimation of vaccine effects. The authors concluded that current evidence supports the efficacy of rhesus rotavirus vaccines, particularly the RRV-TV vaccine, and the human rotavirus vaccine 89-12 in preventing rotavirus diarrhoea and all-cause diarrhoea. However, evidence regarding their safety, as well as their impact on mortality and severe outcomes, remains insufficient and inconclusive. Bovine rotavirus vaccines also demonstrated efficacy, but no safety data were available for these vaccines. The authors emphasized the need for further randomized controlled trials of new rotavirus vaccines, particularly those conducted simultaneously in high-, middle-, and low-income countries, to strengthen the evidence base. It was noted that several vaccines investigated in this review, such as the live attenuated rhesus-human reassortant tetravalent vaccine, are no longer in routine clinical use. Since the review was written in 2004, newer vaccines have been developed, tested, and approved for use. For updated information on currently approved rotavirus vaccines, the authors referred readers to a more recent Cochrane review published in 2010.
